newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Clamour rises over China's plans for HK laws.
newsitem.headline: Clamour rises over China's plans for HK laws.

text.p: In his strongest worded attack yet, Governor Chris Patten lashed out on Thursday at China's "repugnant" proposal to dilute Hong Kong's civil liberties laws, including its bill of rights.
On the eve of a debate in Beijing on the measures, Patten issued a lengthy statement warning the proposed amendments would seriously damage Hong Kong.

His designated successor and Hong Kong's post-colonial leader Tung Chee-hwa, who is visiting Beijing for a crucial meeting to discuss the laws, argued in defence that the international community had misconstrued the situation.

Beijing's plans to repeal or amend a list of 25 Hong Kong laws and ordinances, including parts of its Bill of Rights, has sparked outrage in the British colony and forceful objections from London and its allies.

U.S. President Bill Clinton has expressed concern. Britain summoned the Chinese ambassador in order to lodge a protest and Foreign Minister Malcolm Rifkind plans to pursue the issue in a meeting with his Chinese counterpart Qian Qichen next month.
Qian insisted the transition process to when China resumes sovereignty of Hong Kong at midnight on June 30 was going well.
"During the transitional period, I don't know how many so-called crises of confidence have occurred," Qian said in Beijing. "But as I can see, the situation is now quite good."
But Patten painted a very different picture.
"Nobody who has spent more than a few minutes in Hong Kong over the last few days can be in any doubt that they (the proposals) are repugnant to the community," Patten said.
"On few issues over the years has there been such a clear and broad consensus, embracing almost all shades of the political spectrum," Patten said.

"To these voices have been added those overseas - including not only British Ministers but most recently President Clinton - who wish Hong Kong well, and who want to believe in "one country, two systems", but who are deeply concerned at the prospect Hong Kong's freedoms will be eroded."
Clinton told a White House news conference on Tuesday that Hong Kong might be of much less value to China if the civil liberties of its people were crushed.

"I'm not so sure that it can exist with all of its potential to help China modernise its own economy and open opportunities for its own people, if the civil liberties of the people are crushed," he said.
Responding to Clinton's remarks, Tung told Hong Kong reporters: "I think there are certain sectors of people around the world who are concerned. But I think they are being misled."
"I think they should spend more time to really understand what is really going on in Hong Kong."
He said polls conducted by foreign chambers of commerce in Hong Kong showed a high level of business confidence in Hong Kong's future after the handover to China in mid-1997.
"I wish all those people around the world would spend more time understanding truly what is happening in Hong Kong."
Tung was in Beijing for a two-day meeting of the Preparatory Committee, the 150-strong China-appointed caucus responsible for shaping Hong Kong's future in the countdown to the handover.
The question of the laws is high on the agenda.
Patten dismissed Tung's assertions and argued Clinton's views were widely shared.
"He (Clinton) is not being misinformed about what's going on in Hong Kong," Patten said after he touring an old people's community centre on Hong Kong island.
Patten warned the proposals, if passed, would shatter the "high degree of autonomy" promised to Hong Kong in the 1984 Sino-British Joint Declaration governing the handover.

The treaty embodies Chinese paramount leader Deng Xiaoping's "one country, two systems" vision which promises Hong Kong people will run Hong Kong and will be permitted to maintain their freedoms and capitalist way of life intact for 50 years.

"Hong Kong is entitled to know, before 1 July, whether China still believes in "one country, two systems" or whether it now wants to impose "one country, one system" in contravention of its international obligations and its solemn promises to the six million people of Hong Kong," Patten said.
In Hong Kong, meanwhile, the British passed another milestone on Thursday in the countdown to the end of more than 150 years of colonial rule.
To the drumbeat of a traditional Chinese lion dance, Princess Anne formally opened the new British Consulate in preparation for the handover.
When the red flag of China flutters over Hong Kong on July 1, the official British presence will be contained in the consulate, just one among dozens of consulates in Hong Kong.
